newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges rival China to protect HK freedom.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges rival China to protect HK freedom.

text.p: Taipei on Monday urged rival China to protect Hong Kong's freedoms after the British colony ia handed back at midnight, but reiterated that Taiwan would not be gobbled up by Beijing in the same manner.

Asserting sovereignty on the eve of communist Beijing's historic moment, Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government added it hoped ties between Hong Kong and Taiwan would continue unchanged following the handover.

"We hope the Chinese communists will consider the greater interest and fulfill their promises to the Hong Kong people, and adjust several unrealistic policies and intentions toward Taiwan," government spokesman David Lee said in a formal statement of Taipei's policy on the handover.

Taiwan has repeatedly rejected Beijing's view that Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty under a "one country, two systems" pledge of local autonomy was a model for Taiwan's own eventual "reunification with the motherland".

Taipei says that while Hong Hong has been a British colony for 150 years, Taiwan's exiled Republic China has never lost sovereignty even after losing a civil war on the mainland in 1949 and taking refuge on the island.

Lee said Taipei, which considers Hong Kong a part of the exiled Republic of China that still exists on Taiwan, would not scale back its quasi-official, but substantial presence in Hong Kong after the handover.
"All our offices in Hong Kong will stay on, and strengthen their services to our Hong Kong compatriots," Lee told reporters.
"The Republic of China... will not change its concerns for the Hong Kong compatriots' welfare and freedom because of the change in Hong Kong's status," Lee said.
The cabinet-level Mainland Affairs Council said it would allow Hong Kong to set up a representative office in Taipei after the handover, reciprocating Taipei's current office in the territory.
But the council warned that Beijing's impending reign over Hong Kong, the main conduit for Taiwan's huge investments in China, would increase the communists' power to squeeze Taiwan politically.

"After July 1 Chinese communists will have more chips to play against Taiwan. If we do not have some sense of forewarning, then we are being too optimistic," said William Li, head of the council's Hong Kong affairs department.

Hong Kong is the main transit point for some US$30 billion worth of investment projects that Taiwan businesses have poured into the mainland since cross-strait political tensions began to thaw in the 1980s.
Taiwan bans direct links with China in the absence of official ties. It has adopted laws that regard Hong Kong as a special administrative zone in order to circumvent the ban.

But in a sign of rising caution by Hong Kong toward Taiwan ahead of the retrocession, former Taiwan justice minister Ma Ying-jeou on Monday said Hong Kong had rejected his visa application for a private visit.
"It is very ridiculous. Why is my status as private citizen sensitive?" Ma, who left the government in April, told Reuters.

Handover-induced caution was felt in Taiwan's recently red hot stock market. The benchmark index, which has surged 10 percent in June, clawed to a seven-year high on Monday but gained only 0.06 percent or 5.80 points to 9,030.28.
On the streets of bustling Taipei, people reacted to the handover with a mixture of apathy and cautious optimism.
"It's normal because Hong Kong is a part of China and doesn't really affect us because we are in Taiwan," said Chen Chia-yi, a 22-year-old bakery worker.
"I don't have any feelings about it, but it's right for Hong Kong to go back," said 63-year-old taxi driver Tsai Chin-tang.
